extracted.intended_audience: researchers of peer review and research funding; funding-agency staff and policy-makers interested in grant review criteria
extracted.subtask_description: A systematic-review synthesis of the evaluation criteria peers use when assessing grant applications, identifying 15 evaluation criteria and mapping how they relate to 30 evaluated entities (applicant, project, environment). Intended to inform research on peer review, transparency, and funding-policy design.

rubrics_metrics.name: originality
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of the aims and outcomes of a proposed project in terms of novelty/innovation (e.g. 'originality of the study').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper states that 'The aims and outcomes of a proposed project are assessed in terms of the evaluation criteria originality, academic relevance, and extra-academic relevance.' Example evaluative question: 'Is the project innovative?' The term is used as a dimension to distinguish more meritorious proposals from less meritorious ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: academic relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Judgement of the proposed project's relevance to academic audiences, scholarship, or the discipline (academic importance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed alongside originality and extra-academic relevance as a primary way peers assess aims/outcomes. The authors treat academic relevance as a distinct subtype of relevance used in many included studies and sometimes aggregated with other relevance types for overlap analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: extra-academic relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of the proposed project's relevance or usefulness outside academia (societal, policy, clinical, economic impact).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly named in the synthesis as one of three relevance dimensions applied to aims and outcomes. The authors note that relevance is often split into subtypes (general, academic, extra-academic) and that studies sometimes merge these when analysing overlap.

rubrics_metrics.name: general relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: A higher-level notion of relevance applied to the project as a whole (not distinguished into academic vs extra-academic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors note that some studies report a single 'general relevance' criterion; in overlap calculations they experimented with merging general, academic, and extra-academic relevance to examine study overlap. It functions as a broad relevance/importance dimension.

rubrics_metrics.name: quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation of the intrinsic quality of the proposed research content (e.g. quality of design, methods, theoretical grounding).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appears as a content-level criterion: 'The proposed research process is evaluated both on the content level (quality, appropriateness, rigor, coherence/justification)...' Used to judge substantive merit of research plans rather than merely their description.

rubrics_metrics.name: appropriateness
rubrics_metrics.description: Judgement whether chosen methods, approaches, and resources are suitable for addressing the research question / achieving the aims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as a content-level evaluation criterion describing fit between question, methods, and aims (e.g. 'appropriateness of the research design'). Often operationalized in included studies as 'appropriateness – present/absent' when coding criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: rigor
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of methodological rigor and scientific stringency of the proposed research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly characterised as a content-level criterion (paired with quality, appropriateness, coherence/justification). Rigor is used to capture methodological thoroughness and robustness of research plans.

rubrics_metrics.name: coherence/justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation of logical coherence of the proposal and justification of choices (theoretical and methodological rationale).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of the content-level cluster: assesses whether aims, theory, methods, and outcomes hang together and are properly justified. The authors treat 'coherence/justification' as a single labelled criterion in the synthesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of how clearly the research process, aims, methods, and plans are described in the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as a description-level criterion (distinct from content-level criteria): 'the proposed research process is evaluated ... on the level of description (clarity, completeness)'. Used to evaluate communicative quality rather than substantive content.

rubrics_metrics.name: completeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Judgement whether the application includes all necessary information and fully describes project components (e.g. methods, budget, timeline).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also a description-level criterion: completeness concerns whether required elements are present and sufficiently detailed. Examples in coding included items like 'budget – described, appropriate' which were split into completeness and appropriateness codes.

rubrics_metrics.name: feasibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of whether the resources, timeline, personnel, and methods allow the proposed research to be carried out successfully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors state: 'The resources needed to implement the research process are evaluated in terms of the evaluation criterion feasibility.' Feasibility is typically connected to budget, equipment, timeline, and investigator capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: motivation
rubrics_metrics.description: A psychological evaluation of the applicant's motivation and commitment to the proposed project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identified under applicant-focused criteria: the person and personality of the applicant are assessed from a 'psychological' perspective (motivation, traits). Used in some studies to explain acceptance/rejection decisions and flagged as potentially problematic re: fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: traits
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of applicant personality or personal characteristics (e.g. leadership, perseverance, social skills) relevant to project success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grouped with 'motivation' as the psychological applicant-perspective. Examples in entity coding included social skills, leadership, ability to motivate others; the authors note that these applicant-focused criteria can deviate from impartiality ideals.

rubrics_metrics.name: diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: A sociological appraisal of applicant attributes related to diversity (e.g. demographic, institutional, network diversity) considered relevant to selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as the sociological aspect of applicant appraisal (contrasted with psychological aspects). The authors flag that some applicant-related criteria (including diversity-related judgements) may not conform to fairness doctrines and can introduce bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: soundness
rubrics_metrics.description: General assessment of conceptual and methodological soundness of the proposal (often cited alongside originality, relevance, and feasibility).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in the literature to denote overall scientific robustness (e.g. in the analytical-framework example: 'Grant applications are typically assessed in terms of originality, relevance, soundness, and feasibility'). It functions as a broad dimension capturing methodological and conceptual solidity.
